options.text: In northeastern China, a dance of the Korean community takes its steps from farming. Dancers mime walking the ridges between fields to drums, gongs and the piercing sound of a suona.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Hunan’s Wulingyuan landscape, more than 3,000 sandstone pillars and peaks rise above the ravines. Many individual pillars are taller than 200 metres.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Traditional Chinese block printers prepare smooth planks of pear or jujube wood only two centimetres thick. An image starts on thin paper before an engraver cuts it into the wood.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Listen to vallenato from the Magdalena region and you can hear several histories at once. Cattle herders’ songs, African chants, Indigenous dance rhythms and Spanish verse all helped shape it.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A varnished wooden object from Pasto begins far from the woodshop. Harvesters collect buds in the forests of Putumayo to make the material decorators call mopa-mopa.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Barranquilla’s four days of carnival reflect its past as a Caribbean trading port. Dance traditions from Colombia’s interior met European and African ones there.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Cuban son, the bass helps tell the dancers where to step. Musicians improvise around patterns, drawing lyrics from everyday life and passing songs on by ear.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: After upheavals in Haiti in the 1790s, enslaved people brought tumba francesa to eastern Cuba. Its dances joined French forms with musical traditions from West Africa.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The palaces in Cuba’s city of Trinidad trace the fortunes of sugar. The Brunet and Cantero mansions date from the town’s prosperity in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Ecuadorian pasillo takes its name from the dancers’ “small step.” Its music brings an Andean song tradition together with the waltz, minuet and Spanish bolero.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: About a thousand kilometres off mainland Ecuador, three ocean currents meet around the Galápagos. The islands’ unusual mix of marine life begins with that underwater crossroads.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The finest Ecuadorian toquilla hats take as long as eight months to weave. Workers strip the palm fibre, boil it and dry it before weaving the crown and brim.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Egypt, Coptic Christians and Muslims take part in festivals that commemorate the Holy Family’s flight from Bethlehem. Processions retrace parts of the journey.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The pyramids of Giza belong to a much larger landscape of the dead. Around the old capital of Memphis, it stretches to Dahshur and includes rock-cut tombs and low, flat-roofed mastabas.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Egypt’s Western Desert contains a valley full of early whale fossils. Wadi Al-Hitan preserves the transition from land-dwelling mammals to whales that spent their lives at sea.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Some of the last surviving traditional buildings of the Asante near Kumasi are made from earth, timber and straw. Keeping them standing means caring for materials the rains readily wear away.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A lead singer calls and a chorus answers in Ghanaian highlife. Guitars and horns can share the rhythm with drums and xylophones, in songs drawn from daily life.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A Ghanaian kente cloth can have a proverb for a name. Weavers make narrow strips on horizontal looms, choosing patterns and colours that can signal who will wear the fabric.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Starting in 930, people gathered outdoors at Þingvellir for two weeks a year to make laws and settle disputes. The assembly met there for more than eight centuries.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Eight of the ten central volcanoes in Vatnajökull National Park lie under ice. When water escapes the glacier’s edge, the sudden flood has an Icelandic name, jökulhlaup.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Icelandic towns have turned heated outdoor pools into gathering places year-round. A soak in a public hot tub can be as much an occasion for conversation as for swimming.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At a Sankirtana performance in Manipur, the audience sits around the performers. Two drummers and a small group of singers and dancers tell stories of Krishna in a hall or courtyard.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The builders of Ramappa Temple in Telangana put porous “floating bricks” high in its tower. Using lighter bricks reduced the weight that the carved stone below had to carry.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: During Navaratri in Gujarat, garba dancers circle an oil lamp inside a perforated earthen pot, or an image of the goddess Amba. The circle moves anticlockwise to singing and clapping.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A Papuan noken bag can carry a baby, a catch of fish or a load of firewood. Knotted or woven from plant fibres, it can also be presented as a peace offering.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Wayang puppet theatre flourished both in village performances and at the royal courts of Java and Bali. As it spread to other islands, each developed its own music and styles of puppetry.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Prambanan in Java, three temples honour Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma, and three others honour the animals that serve them. Scenes from the Ramayana run along the temple walls.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At the January feast in Chiapa de Corzo, the word parachicos names both the dancers and the dance they perform in honour of the saints.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At the foot of Popocatépetl, houses in Puebla wear tiles on the outside. Their glazed walls are as much part of the historic city as its cathedral.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At El Tajín near the Gulf coast, a pyramid is named for the niches that cover its sides. This city rose to prominence after the fall of Teotihuacan.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Four Quechua-speaking communities rebuild the Q’eswachaka rope bridge over the Apurímac gorge every year. The rebuilding itself is one of the ties between the villages.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On the coast in Ica, Christmas dance groups tell the story of the shepherds and the Wise Men through two complementary traditions, Hatajo de Negritos and Hatajo de Pallitas.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Moquegua, Sarawja marks the end of the rainy season and the beginning of harvest. Groups called ruedas, or wheels, dance in circles or parallel rows.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Beqa, Sawau firewalkers trace their gift to an ancestor who went looking for an eel. In the story, the creature he caught could speak and offered him power over fire in return for its freedom.
options.label: Source

options.text: A Fijian drua carries its crew across the ocean on two hulls. The deck between them turns two slender canoe bodies into a platform for long-distance sailing.
options.label: Source

options.text: Fiji’s first colonial capital was Levuka on Ovalau. Its old port still follows the beach in a low line of buildings among mango and coconut trees.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the southern highlands, Huli men grew their own hair to make wigs. An example in Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum is decorated with everlasting flowers.
options.label: Source

options.text: A large Iatmul canoe on the Sepik often has a crocodile for a prow. The carver shapes the head directly at the front of the wooden vessel.
options.label: Source

options.text: Highland farmers at Kuk left their oldest field plans buried in a swamp. Their ditches and planting surfaces show that agriculture developed independently in New Guinea thousands of years ago.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Rennell, what used to be a coral atoll’s lagoon is now Lake Tegano. The whole atoll was lifted above the sea, leaving a lake where seawater once lay.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Bamboo supplies whole ensembles in the Solomon Islands. Musicians turn stems into tuned panpipes, so players with different lengths of pipe can carry different parts of a tune.
options.label: Source

options.text: In lagoons off Malaita, families built islands by bringing pieces of reef rock back in canoes. The ground beneath a village could be the accumulated work of generations.
options.label: Source

options.text: A Cook Islands tīvaevae in Te Papa’s collection has a design its maker used for seven wedding quilts. She changed the colours each time she sewed it.
options.label: Source

options.text: A travelling companion of Māori ancestors left a genetic trail across the Pacific. DNA from kiore, the Pacific rat, links early New Zealand populations with lineages in the Cook and Society islands.
options.label: Source

options.text: On Manihiki, one of the northern atolls, the lagoon serves as a farm. Cultivating oysters for pearls became one of the island’s principal commercial activities.
options.label: Source

options.text: On Yap, stone money can change hands without moving. For the largest carved rings, the community recognises the new owner while the stone stays where it was.
options.label: Source

options.text: Off Pohnpei, people built Nan Madol across a network of artificial islets. Basalt walls still mark the ceremonial compounds, with canoe channels where a town on land might have streets.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the outlying islands of Yap State, the craft of building a sailing canoe is passed on alongside the skill of finding land. Navigators learn to read waves, weather and the night sky.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A CHamoru latte stone comes in two parts. A bowl-shaped cap rests on a stone pillar, and rows of these supports once held buildings above the ground.
options.label: Source

options.text: When an introduced snake wiped out most of Guam’s forest birds, trees lost their seed couriers. Researchers found native seeds no longer reaching damaged forest from intact stands as they did on neighbouring islands.
options.label: Source

options.text: CHamoru sailors built outrigger canoes so fast that European visitors nicknamed them “flying proas.” A large seagoing form is known on Guam as a sakman.
options.label: Source

options.text: On Pentecost Island, the yam harvest is marked by land diving. Participants leap from wooden towers with vines tied to their ankles.
options.label: Source

options.text: Oral traditions about Chief Roi Mata tie together three islands. Archaeologists found physical evidence at sites remembered as his home, the place he died and his burial ground.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A drawing in sand can cross a language boundary in Vanuatu. Communities speaking dozens of languages have shared a way of tracing patterns to communicate and pass on stories.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Taputapuātea on Raiatea, sacred gathering grounds face a lagoon and a passage through the reef. The site connected Polynesian communities whose visitors had to cross the ocean to meet.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Fakarava, thousands of camouflage groupers gather in a reef pass to spawn around the full moon. For a brief window, divers can see fish normally spread across the reef packed together.
options.label: Source

options.text: In 1769 James Cook watched Venus cross the face of the Sun from Tahiti. His drawing records the planet as a little black disc against the bright Sun.
options.label: NASA

options.text: Among Palau’s Rock Islands are lakes of seawater cut off from the open ocean. Some have developed their own distinctive jellyfish populations.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A Palauan bai is a meeting house that can also be read. Painted scenes on its timbers preserve stories for the people gathering beneath them.
options.label: Source

options.text: Palauan chiefs could declare a bul, closing an area to harvesting so it could recover. That customary practice helped shape the islands’ system of protected waters.
options.label: Source

options.text: Kiribati once had different calendar dates at opposite ends of the country. In 1995 it changed how its islands reckoned the date so they could share the same working day.
options.label: Source

options.text: The eight islands of the Phoenix group give only a hint of the landscape below. The protected waters around them also contain great seamounts that never break the surface.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Traditional armour from Kiribati used materials an atoll could supply. A shirt of thick coconut fibre could be worn with a helmet made from the spiny skin of a porcupinefish.
options.label: Source

options.text: A Marshallese navigation chart records something a coastline map leaves out. Curved sticks show how ocean swells bend and cross around islands.
options.label: Source

options.text: In 1946 a fleet of more than seventy ships lay anchored at Bikini Atoll as targets for a nuclear test. The lagoon became a graveyard for part of that fleet.
options.label: Source

options.text: To make a ceremonial dress mat called a jaki-ed, weavers boil and dry a particular kind of pandanus leaf. Beating it releases fibres fine enough to weave into clothing.
options.label: Source

options.text: Mining the phosphate from Nauru’s interior uncovered a forest of sharp limestone pinnacles. Much of the plateau was left too rugged for homes or farming.
options.label: Source

options.text: Nauruans have a tradition of catching and taming frigatebirds. These ocean-going birds, known locally as itsi, have a place in island life beyond their visits to the coast.
options.label: Source

options.text: The Nauruan flag is a miniature map. The line marks the equator, the star sits south of it like the island, and its twelve points recall the traditional tribes.
options.label: Source

options.text: Before dawn, a kagu can announce itself with a bark. This grey, ground-dwelling bird lives wild only in New Caledonia.
options.label: Source

options.text: New Caledonian crows make tools with hooks. Researchers watched wild birds fashion hooked implements and use them to reach food they could not grasp with their beaks.
options.label: Source

options.text: New Caledonia’s barrier reefs enclose lagoons with room for dugongs. These plant-eating relatives of manatees live alongside turtles and whales in the reef system.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Niue gets rain but has no permanent rivers running across its surface. Water drains through the porous coral limestone that makes up the island.
options.label: Source

options.text: Niuean hiapo is cloth made from bark. Nineteenth-century artists drew fine designs on it freehand, turning the pale surface into an intricate patterned sheet.
options.label: Source

options.text: A Niuean fisher could head out in a small vaka with an outrigger for stability. A common form carries just one or two people along the coast.
options.label: Source

options.text: A Samoan fine mat can feel almost like silk. Weavers split pandanus leaves into exceptionally narrow strips, and the completed mat can be exchanged at major family occasions.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A traditional Samoan tattooist works with a kit of comb-like tools. A second tool taps the pigment-bearing teeth into the skin to build the pattern.
options.label: Source

options.text: A Samoan fale can be a home, kitchen or meeting place. In an open-sided fale, the posts carry the roof and the breeze can pass right through the building.
options.label: Source

options.text: On Tuvalu’s coral atolls, growers raise pulaka, a giant swamp taro, down in dug pits. The gardens bring its roots close to freshwater beneath the island surface.
options.label: Source

options.text: Tuvalu’s game of te ano is played with two balls. The hard balls are traditionally made from pandanus leaves.
options.label: Source

options.text: In the 1890s an expedition brought drilling equipment to Funafuti to test how coral atolls form. The layers beneath the island offered a way to investigate a question Darwin had raised.
options.label: Source

options.text: On Tinian, the House of Taga is marked by immense latte stones. The pillars and caps survive as foundations for a building whose wooden superstructure has gone.
options.label: Source

options.text: The three islets of Maug are pieces of one volcanic rim. Sail between them and the water below you fills an ancient caldera.
options.label: Source

options.text: Carolinian master navigators helped keep long-distance canoe voyaging alive in the Northern Marianas after Spanish colonisation disrupted CHamoru seafaring.
options.label: Source

options.text: Tonga’s 2022 Hunga eruption sent a pressure wave ringing around Earth. Instruments continued to register its passage as it circled the globe over several days.
options.label: NOAA

options.text: The Haʻamonga ʻa Maui on Tongatapu looks like a giant stone doorway. Its two upright posts and crosspiece are all slabs of coral limestone.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A Tongan lakalaka is a speech you can watch. Performers stand in rows, singing and clapping while their movements deliver meaning alongside the words.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Three customary kingdoms share this one French territory. ʻUvea occupies Wallis, while Alo and Sigave divide Futuna.
options.label: Source

options.text: Wallis has lakes but no surface river network. Rain filters into the ground, while old volcanic craters such as Lalolalo hold pools of standing water.
options.label: Source

options.text: On Wallis and Futuna, makers beat the inner bark of the paper mulberry into sheets of tapa. It becomes a cloth that can be painted without weaving a single thread.
options.label: Source

options.text: Traditional Hawaiian fishponds have a gate called a mākāhā. Water and small fish can pass between its slats, while larger fish stay in the pond.
options.label: Source

options.text: The mark between the last two vowels in Hawaiʻi is a consonant. Called the ʻokina, it signals a glottal stop. A line over a vowel, the kahakō, changes how long the vowel is held.
options.label: Source

options.text: The Hawaiian chain records the motion of an ocean plate. Volcanoes grow over a hot spot and are carried northwest, so islands farther along the chain are generally older.
options.label: Source

options.text: Bagana builds its cone with thick lava that creeps down its flanks. Eruptions have been recorded on this Bougainville volcano since the nineteenth century.
options.label: Source

options.text: One variety of Rotokas, spoken on Bougainville, distinguishes just six consonant sounds. It is one of the smallest consonant inventories linguists have described.
options.label: Source

options.text: In bamboo bands on Bougainville and nearby Buka, players strike tuned tubes with rubber cut from footwear. A worn sandal can find a second life as a musical instrument.
options.label: Source

options.text: Rural Cheshire was quiet enough for Jodrell Bank to listen to space. Radar echoes were already helping researchers study cosmic rays there in 1945.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Ironbridge in Shropshire, the iron industry put its product on display in the most literal way. The bridge across the Severn was built of cast iron.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Cornish miners carried their hard-rock mining skills overseas. The engine houses standing above Cornwall's mines have relatives on mining landscapes on other continents.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: People lived on St Kilda's Atlantic cliffs for over 2,000 years. The last residents left in 1930, but their stone storehouses still stand among the seabird colonies.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the far north, a blanket of peat spreads over the Flow Country. Thousands of years of partly decomposed plants have locked carbon into this wet ground.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At New Lanark, cotton mill owner Robert Owen made schooling part of village life and established an infant school for the workers' children.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The steps at the Giant's Causeway are the ends of basalt columns. They split into polygonal shapes as a mass of ancient lava cooled.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Belfast's shipbuilders built Titanic beside her sister ship Olympic. A giant gantry straddled their slipways.
options.label: www.titanicbelfast.com

options.text: The rope bridge to Carrick-a-Rede began as a way to get to work. Salmon fishermen crossed the gap to reach the island.
options.label: www.nationaltrust.org.uk

options.text: At Pontcysyllte you can steer a canal boat across the River Dee without entering the river. A cast-iron trough carries the canal high over the valley.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Slate cut out of the mountains of northwest Wales ended up on roofs around the world. Railways connected the quarries to the coast.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Blaenavon the ironworks, workers' houses, mines and transport routes survive together. You can trace how a Welsh hillside was turned into iron.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: People were mining salt near Hallstatt in the second millennium BCE. The town beside the lake owes much of its wealth to the mountain behind it.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Semmering Railway crosses the Alps on viaducts and through tunnels laid out in the 1800s, while steam locomotives were still a young invention.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Vienna's Spanish Riding School passes on its work with Lipizzaner horses through generations of riders. Learning includes caring for the horses as well as riding them.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: More than thirty granite cairns mark Bronze Age burials at Sammallahdenmäki. People piled those stones up more than three thousand years ago.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Fiddlers in Kaustinen pass dance tunes on by ear. Several hundred local tunes belong to a tradition more than 250 years old.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Finnish has a word for the steam that rises when water hits hot sauna stones. Löyly is central to what makes a sauna a sauna.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The great passage tombs beside the Boyne were already standing thousands of years before Ireland's medieval castles. Carved stones mark the entrances to a landscape built for the dead.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Irish mythology gives the hero Cú Chulainn a hurley. The stick-and-ball game he plays survives on pitches across Ireland today.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Irish uilleann pipes take their air from bellows worked with an elbow, leaving the player's mouth free while the pipes sound.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Water has dissolved more than 900 caves into a small area of gypsum in the northern Apennines. Some go deeper than 250 metres.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Bologna, porticoes link one building to the next. Over the centuries these sheltered walkways evolved into a network stretching for dozens of kilometres.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Rome built the Appian Way as a military road. Its eventual destination was Brindisi, the Adriatic port from which armies could sail east.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In western Latvia, Suiti women sing over a sustained vocal drone. Their Catholic community has kept the tradition in a largely Lutheran region.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Riga's streets preserve two very different building fashions side by side, elaborate Art Nouveau façades and nineteenth-century wooden houses.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Kuldīga still follows the street plan it had when it helped govern the Duchy of Courland. Its log buildings show how local carpenters borrowed ideas from across the Baltic.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Take the shortest route from Liechtenstein to an ocean and you still have to cross two national borders. Even its neighbours are landlocked.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The country took its name from the family that bought its lands. The family in turn took its name from a castle in Austria.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: A British visitor can hum along to Liechtenstein's national anthem on a first hearing. It uses the tune of God Save the King.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: A Lithuanian sodas is a garden you can hang above a cradle. Its makers thread rye straw into geometric shapes to wish the child well.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: When Kaunas unexpectedly became Lithuania's temporary capital between the world wars, it had to build the institutions of a capital virtually from scratch.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Lithuanian sutartinės, singers weave together different melodies and rhythms. The name comes from a verb meaning to agree or be in harmony.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Pilgrims hop through Echternach every Pentecost Tuesday. The procession survived repeated bans and has been documented since around 1100.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Successive European powers kept strengthening Luxembourg City's fortifications. Its rocky promontory became a fortress built in layers by its own conquerors.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Luxembourg's name grew out of the name of a small fortress. The modern country's capital grew up around its site.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In Štip a spring tradition calls for climbing a hill with forty pebbles. At the top, participants make wishes and throw thirty-nine into the river below.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Dancers in Dramche cross their hands and grip their neighbours' belts. The middle dancer balances the two halves of the semicircle as they move.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Lake Ohrid has been isolated long enough for animals to evolve there that live nowhere else. The lake and the old town on its shore share a World Heritage listing.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The chambers of the Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum were cut down into solid rock. Some imitate architectural details of Malta's temples above ground.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Malta's flat ftira is sourdough, despite a name derived from an Arabic word for unleavened bread. The split loaf might hold tuna, capers and tomato.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Prehistoric builders on Malta and Gozo raised temples out of immense stone blocks. Several have rooms shaped like lobes around a central passage.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Mileștii Mici the wine collection is measured in millions of bottles. The underground galleries hold a Guinness record for the size of the cellar's collection.
options.label: www.guinnessworldrecords.com

options.text: To find the river that gave Moldova its name, look across the border in Romania.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Moldova's anthem began as a twelve-stanza poem. The sung version skips from stanza two to five, then to nine and twelve.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Monaco holds a particular geographical distinction. It takes up less land than any other country with a coast.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: A Genoese fortress built in 1215 stood on the rock of Monaco. The Grimaldis first captured it in 1297, more than a century before securing it for good.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Although French is widely spoken in Monaco, the official words of its national anthem are in Monégasque.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In Durmitor, glacial lakes sit high above the gorges. The Tara River has cut a canyon deep into the mountains below them.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Kotor's Boka Navy traces its history to 809 and a saint's relics arriving by sea. Its members still assemble for ceremonial dances.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The bay of Kotor once exported skills as well as goods. Its schools of masonry and icon painting influenced artists elsewhere on the Adriatic.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Franeker a wool worker built a working model of the solar system into the ceiling of his living room. Eise Eisinga's planets still move.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Schokland used to be an island in the Zuiderzee. Drainage left it stranded in the middle of farmland.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The windmills at Kinderdijk helped keep farmland dry. They lifted water in stages so it could drain out when the river level allowed.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Rjukan and Notodden, Norwegian waterfalls helped make fertiliser. Hydroelectricity powered factories that drew nitrogen from the air.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On the rocks around Alta Fjord, generations of people painted and engraved thousands of images over a span of several millennia.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Urnes, Viking carving traditions and Romanesque church architecture meet in one building made of wood.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Prehistoric miners at Krzemionki dug shafts and galleries in search of striped flint. Some of what they mined became polished axe heads.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Tarnowskie Góry, water pumped out to keep the mines dry found a second use. It supplied drinking water to people above ground.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Two Lutheran Churches of Peace in Silesia rank as Europe's largest timber-framed religious buildings. They grew out of the settlement that ended the Thirty Years' War.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Ice Age artists in the Côa Valley carved animals on exposed riverside rock. Their outdoor gallery survived for thousands of years.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Look at the contours of the Alto Douro and you can trace centuries of winemaking in the terraces cut into its steep banks.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Potters at Bisalhães crush clay with a wooden hammer, smooth their pots with pebbles and fire them to the black finish for which the village is known.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Roșia Montană, Roman miners cut an underground network into the mountains by hand to reach gold. Kilometres of their galleries survive.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Brâncuși stretched a war memorial across the town of Târgu Jiu. An avenue links sculptures in two parks on a single axis.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In northern Moldavia, biblical scenes cover the outside walls of churches. Worshippers could read the painted stories before they ever stepped indoors.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On the Lena River in Siberia, water works like a wedge. Repeated freezing and thawing helped separate cliffs into ranks of enormous stone pillars.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A major wild reindeer migration crosses the Putorana Plateau, where Arctic tundra and northern forest meet above the Arctic Circle.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Ice Age artists in Shulgan-Tash Cave painted a two-humped camel alongside mammoths and woolly rhinoceroses in what is now the southern Urals.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: San Marino traces its founding to a stonemason named Marinus who, according to tradition, settled on Mount Titano in the year 301.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: San Marino's medieval walls still follow the ridgeline of Mount Titano. Three towers stand above the tiny republic's historic centre.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: There are no official words to sing to San Marino's national anthem. Its melody draws on a chorale dating back to the tenth century.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Slovak shepherds played a flute about as tall as a person. The fujara can be two metres long, yet its player uses just three finger holes.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Slovak wireworkers once repaired cracked household pots by binding them in wire. The repair technique grew into a decorative craft of its own.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Banská Štiavnica a mining town reshaped its watershed. Reservoirs and channels collected the water that helped power its mining machinery.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Slovenian beekeepers keep colonies in bee houses. Painted front panels turn rows of hives into miniature galleries.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Reka River disappears into the Škocjan Caves, where it runs through an immense underground canyon.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: During Shrovetide near Ptuj, bands of Kurenti visit houses and jump in the yard. Their clanging bells are meant to chase away evil.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At the Vizcaya Bridge near Bilbao, passengers cross the river in a gondola hanging from the bridge. Ships can pass beneath its high iron span.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Menorca's prehistoric communities built entire settlements and tombs out of massive stones. Some structures still line up with one another across the island.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The red pinnacles of Las Médulas are the remains of Roman gold mining. Engineers channelled water into the hills to break them apart.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The 404 cottages around Gammelstad's church had an unusual purpose. Distant parishioners slept in them when they could not make the round trip to worship in a day.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Grimeton, six steel towers carried early wireless messages across the Atlantic. The original 1920s transmitting equipment was kept in working order.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Farmers in Hälsingland once commissioned painted rooms especially for festivities. Some built whole separate houses for those occasions.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Sardona the mountains display older rock resting on top of younger rock. A continental collision pushed enormous slices of crust over one another.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Watchmaking shaped the streets of La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle. After fires, the towns rebuilt in parallel strips that mixed workshops with homes.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Fossils on Monte San Giorgio record a tropical lagoon. Marine reptiles swam there more than 200 million years before their remains sat high above Lake Lugano.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Potters in Kosiv scratch designs through white clay to the grey clay underneath. Metal oxides give the finished ceramics their characteristic greens and yellows.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Ukrainian households, borscht recipes pass through families. Beetroot gives the soup its familiar colour, but no single recipe defines it.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the Ukrainian Carpathians, builders raised domed churches from horizontal logs. Related tserkvas across the border in Poland belong to the same mountain tradition.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Saint Peter's Square has curved colonnades that open towards Rome. The space in front of the basilica is a substantial part of an entire country.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Vatican City became a state in 1929 through an agreement with Italy, decades after the popes lost the last of the old Papal States.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The treaty creating Vatican City even provided for a railway station. Italy agreed to connect the tiny state's tracks to its own national network.
options.label: www.vaticanstate.va

options.text: Water entering Kosovo's Nerodimka river system can leave for two different seas. One branch feeds the Danube and Black Sea, the other the Vardar and Aegean.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Kosovo adopted a wordless anthem in 2008 so choosing lyrics would not privilege one ethnic community over another.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: At Gračanica and other medieval church sites in Kosovo, Byzantine and western Romanesque traditions meet in the architecture and painted interiors.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Pico, grapevines grow in tiny enclosures walled with black volcanic stone. The walls shield them from sea wind and salt spray.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Angra on Terceira was a calling point for sailing ships crossing the Atlantic. Its harbour helped make these remote islands a junction of ocean trade routes.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Capelinhos eruption in 1957 began offshore and added fresh land to Faial. A coastal lighthouse found itself beside an entirely new piece of island.
options.label: volcano.si.edu

options.text: Gibraltar's Gorham's Cave complex preserves traces of Neanderthal life on the Mediterranean coast. The Rock sheltered people long before anyone fortified it.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Gibraltar's name recalls a person. Jabal Tariq, or Tariq's mountain, refers to the commander who took the peninsula in 711.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 transferred Gibraltar from Spain to Britain. The territory sits at the narrow passage between Atlantic and Mediterranean waters.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Victor Hugo made his home in exile at Hauteville House on Guernsey. He designed its extraordinary interiors and worked on Les Misérables there.
options.label: www.maisonsvictorhugo.paris.fr

options.text: Guernsey's Little Chapel is covered in pieces of broken china, pebbles and shells. Even its tiny passages are part of the mosaic.
options.label: www.visitguernsey.com

options.text: Saint Peter Port and Saint Peter in the Wood both honour the patron saint of fishermen. Their names tell you which parish faces the harbour.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: On Tynwald Hill, the island's parliament still holds an outdoor sitting. New laws are proclaimed in Manx and English.
options.label: www.tynwald.org.im

options.text: Manx is spoken again by children on the Isle of Man, following a revival that continued after the last traditional native speaker died.
options.label: courier.unesco.org

options.text: Off the island's southwestern tip sits a much smaller island with a fitting name, the Calf of Man. It is a sanctuary for birds.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: At low tide visitors can walk out to Elizabeth Castle from Jersey. When the water returns, it cuts off the route to the fortress.
options.label: www.jerseyheritage.org

options.text: At La Hougue Bie you can go inside a Neolithic passage grave. A grass-covered mound hides the stone chamber underground.
options.label: www.jerseyheritage.org

options.text: Jersey's connection to the British Crown goes back to the Duchy of Normandy. These islands remained attached to the Crown after most of Normandy was lost.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Madeira preserves a large surviving stretch of the laurel forest that once spread widely through southern Europe. Mist helps sustain it in the island's mountains.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Some of Madeira's walking trails follow levadas. These narrow channels move water across the mountains to land that needs irrigation.
options.label: www.visitmadeira.com

options.text: On the steep streets below Monte, two runners steer a wicker sledge downhill on wooden runners. The ride began as a form of local transport.
options.label: visitmadeira.com

options.text: Sardinia's 'fairy houses' are prehistoric tombs. People cut chambers into rock and fashioned them to resemble the spaces of the living.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Barumini, Bronze Age builders stacked enormous stones into defensive towers called nuraghi. A village grew up around the central stronghold.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Four Sardinian tenore singers stand close in a circle. One sings a poem while the other three build a chorus that includes two remarkably deep, throaty voices.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Could you cross all seven bridges of Königsberg exactly once? Euler's proof that you could not helped launch graph theory. The city is now Kaliningrad.
options.label: old.maa.org

options.text: The Curonian Spit is a long strip of sand shared with Lithuania. People planted it to stop dunes migrating across its settlements.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Baltic shore near Kaliningrad holds great deposits of amber. The material prized by jewellers began as resin oozing from ancient trees.
options.label: www.gia.edu

options.text: Etna's long record of observed eruptions stretches back millennia. Its slopes have helped scientists work out how volcanoes behave.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The floors of Villa Romana del Casale preserve an immense collection of Roman mosaics. A visitor can follow scenes across room after room of the villa.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Eight towns in southeastern Sicily were rebuilt after the earthquake of 1693. The disaster left an entire region with a recognisably Baroque face.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Åland Islands are part of Finland, but Swedish is their sole official language. The archipelago also has its own autonomous government and is demilitarised.
options.label: visitaland.com

options.text: The four-masted Pommern in Mariehamn harbour once carried grain from Australia to England under sail.
options.label: visitaland.com

options.text: Åland is still growing out of the Baltic. Its highest ground emerged around ten thousand years ago as the land rose after the ice sheets retreated.
options.label: visitaland.com

options.text: A small electric railway carries visitors inside New Athos Cave. For decades the underground train was a specially built model from Riga.
options.label: explore-georgia.ge

options.text: High above Abkhazia's Black Sea coast, a rockslide dammed a mountain river. The water that backed up behind it became Lake Ritsa.
options.label: explore-georgia.ge

options.text: Archaeologists at coastal Pitsunda found the remains of a wooden Roman fortress and a later stone fort. This stretch of Black Sea shore was once a Roman frontier.
options.label: www.georgianencyclopedia.ge

options.text: Transnistria issued coins you could recognise by shape and colour. The green three-ruble piece was square with rounded corners.
options.label: www.old.ipn.md

options.text: At Bender, an Ottoman fortress on the Dniester hosted an unlikely guest. Sweden's King Charles XII took refuge in the area after losing at Poltava.
options.label: moldova.travel

options.text: At Dubăsari, the river that gives Transnistria its name also supplies electricity. A hydroelectric dam spans the Dniester there.
options.label: moldova.travel

options.text: Corsican paghjella singing builds in a fixed order. One voice starts the melody, a bass joins, and the highest voice enters last, making use of the echo.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Fango runs from Corsican mountains inhabited by mouflon and bearded vultures down to a Mediterranean gulf. A single watershed links their cliffs to coastal wetlands.
options.label: www.unesco.org

options.text: Scandola's red cliffs are remnants of volcanic rock. Protected waters around the peninsula shelter marine life below the cliffs where seabirds nest.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Svalbard's seed vault stores backups of collections held elsewhere. If refrigeration ever stops, the frozen mountain around the vault buys time for the seeds.
options.label: www.seedvault.no

options.text: Svalbard has its own stocky, short-legged reindeer. It spends the brief Arctic summer building up reserves for the long winter.
options.label: npolar.no

options.text: Glaciers cover roughly three-fifths of Svalbard. On Nordaustlandet, entire ice caps spread across the island.
options.label: publicdata.npolar.no

options.text: At Göbekli Tepe, hunter-gatherers raised monumental T-shaped pillars and carved wild animals into them roughly eleven thousand years ago.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Karagöz shadow theatre, a puppeteer lights translucent figures from behind. The quarrels between Karagöz and Hacivat play out on a screen.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Sardis was the capital of Lydia, a kingdom associated with some of the earliest coins. Its rulers lie beneath huge burial mounds nearby.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In a Cypriot tsiattista duel the competitors improvise verses at each other. A quick answer has to fit the rhythm as well as land its point.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The plain exteriors of churches in the Troodos Mountains hide walls covered in Byzantine paintings.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Lefkara, needleworkers build lace patterns by drawing threads out of linen and embroidering directly into the open spaces.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Kazakh orteke a musician plays a two-stringed dombyra while strings on the same hand make a wooden mountain goat dance on a drum.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Birds flying from Africa and South Asia to breed in Siberia can meet at the same stopover, the lakes of Kazakhstan's northern steppe.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The pieces in the Kazakh game of assyk come from sheep. Players flick an ankle bone to knock other bones out of position.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Parts of western Bahrain are covered in prehistoric burial mounds. Nearly 12,000 survive in the listed fields, and some royal tombs had two storeys.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Bahrain's pearling crews left behind a musical tradition called fjiri. Among its percussion instruments is a clay pot.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Bahrain's old pearl route connects oyster beds offshore with merchants' houses in Muharraq. Following it takes you from the seabed to the people who sold the pearls.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: In Dhaka, a pedal rickshaw doubles as a moving painting. Artists decorate the vehicles by hand, turning ordinary journeys into a street exhibition.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Jamdani weavers create motifs as they weave the cloth, adding individual threads into fine cotton by hand.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Dhaka's Bengali New Year procession grew out of an initiative by art students. Large colourful figures move through the streets with the marchers.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Kampong Ayer much of town life takes place above the Brunei River. Homes stand on stilts and people get around by walkways and water taxis.
options.label: www.bruneitourism.com

options.text: A strip of Malaysia divides Brunei in two. Temburong, the eastern part, has no land connection to the rest of the country within Brunei's borders.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Brunei's sultans once ruled far beyond the little state on today's map. Their influence extended from northwest Borneo into the southern Philippines.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: High Island's enormous hexagonal rock columns began in a volcano. They formed as hot volcanic material cooled and contracted.
options.label: www.geopark.gov.hk

options.text: Hong Kong includes more than two hundred islands as well as a piece of mainland China. Hong Kong Island itself is only one part of the territory.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The territory Britain acquired in 1842 was just Hong Kong Island. Kowloon was added later, and the New Territories came under a 99-year lease.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The Trans-Iranian Railway crosses two mountain ranges to join the Caspian Sea to the Persian Gulf. Its route runs through four climatic zones.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The pattern of caravanserais across Iran traces where travellers could find water and safety. These inns made long journeys by caravan possible.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Hawraman, terraced villages cling to the Zagros Mountains. The steep slopes shaped both the architecture and seasonal movements of the people living there.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Under Maresha and Bet-Guvrin lie chambers cut for everything from oil presses to pigeon breeding. A whole working landscape survives beneath the fields.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Ancient desert towns in the Negev owed their fortunes to incense. Caravans carried frankincense and myrrh west towards Mediterranean ports.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Tel Aviv's White City records a migration of architectural ideas. European-trained designers adapted modernist buildings to the Mediterranean climate.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The southern Iraqi marshes and the ruins of ancient Mesopotamian cities share one World Heritage site. Reeds, water and settlements all belong to the delta's history.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Erbil's citadel rises on a mound formed by one generation building over the remains of another. Its elevation is itself an archaeological record.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Samarra, the Great Mosque's minaret curls upwards. A spiral ramp wraps around its outside.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A pansori singer and one drummer can sustain an epic for hours. The singer moves between narration, dialogue and song.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Korea's tidal flats supply food for migratory shorebirds crossing East Asia. The land they depend on disappears underwater with each tide.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: People kept carving into the rock beside Bangucheon Stream for millennia. On the same stretch of cliffs, prehistoric art sits alongside historical inscriptions.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Pyongyang's cold buckwheat noodles come in a brass bowl. One way to finish the dish is to pour the liquid from radish kimchi over them.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The wall paintings inside Koguryo tombs show clothing, customs and everyday life. Much of what survives of this kingdom's painting is underground.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Mount Kumgang's pale granite peaks have attracted Buddhist communities for centuries. Hermitages and carvings are tucked among its waterfalls and ravines.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Umm Al-Jimāl, villagers reused Roman military buildings and collected scarce water to raise animals and crops in a landscape of dark basalt.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Mansaf layers thin bread, rice or bulgur, and meat cooked in yoghurt on one communal platter. Preparing the feast is itself a social occasion.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Wadi Rum's sandstone landscape doubles as an archive. Generations of travellers and residents carved inscriptions and images into its rock.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Some Japanese kofun look like giant keyholes from above. Those distinctively shaped mounds near Osaka were tombs for members of the elite.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Bunraku theatre several puppeteers can work a single character together while a narrator voices the story to a shamisen accompaniment.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Sado Island's gold mines preserve evidence of different ways to extract precious metal, from washing it out of deposits to cutting underground workings by hand.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Tripoli has a boomerang-shaped exhibition hall about 750 metres long. Brazilian architect Oscar Niemeyer designed it for an international fair.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Bakers press their fingertips into man'ouché dough before topping it with thyme, sumac, sesame and olive oil for breakfast.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Cedars of God preserve a remnant of Lebanon's ancient mountain forests. Cedar timber from this region was prized across the ancient Mediterranean.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: More than two thousand stone jars dot a plateau in Laos. Iron Age communities used them in funerary practices.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Lao khaen looks like a bundle of bamboo pipes. Each tube contains a metal reed, letting one player sound several notes together.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Vat Phou, ancient planners laid out a route from mountain to plain through temples and waterworks, giving the landscape a religious axis.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In kok boru, two teams on horseback compete to carry an ulak into the opposing goal. Traditionally the object in play was a goat carcass.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Sulaiman-Too's five peaks rise over Osh. For more than fifteen hundred years the mountain served as both a sacred place and a landmark on the Silk Roads.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Kyrgyz felt carpets can be made by cutting contrasting sheets of felt together and exchanging the pieces. Two complementary patterns come out of one cut.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The spheres of Kuwait City's best-known towers have a practical origin. The towers were designed as part of the city's fresh-water distribution system.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: A Kuwaiti diwaniya can meet in a home or even a tent. It gives neighbours a regular place to discuss everything from family matters to elections.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Kuwait's Al Sadu Society brought traditional weaving into classrooms by teaching the teachers first. Finished student textiles go on display at Sadu House.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On a bend of the Ayeyarwady at Bagan, the plain is studded with Buddhist temples and stupas built when it was an imperial capital.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Myanmar's Thingyan New Year festivities include pouring water on Buddha images. In some communities younger people also give their elders manicures and pedicures.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The ancient Pyu cities used moats, walls and waterworks in the dry zone of Myanmar. The surviving outlines are big enough to trace entire cities.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Bronze Age communities on the Mongolian steppe stood up stones engraved with stylised deer. Some of these ceremonial stones reach four metres high.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Biyelgee dances fit inside a herder's ger. Dancers can perform half-seated or cross-legged, using shoulders and hands to act out everyday work.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The carved head atop a morin khuur fiddle gives the instrument its familiar name, the horsehead fiddle. Its two strings are played with a bow.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Historic Maldivian mosques were built of coral carved into interlocking blocks. Builders used reef material much as mainland masons used quarried stone.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: From above, the Maldives resolve into chains of coral islands grouped in 26 natural atolls. Dry land is only a tiny part of the archipelago.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: One proposed origin for the name Maldives is a Sanskrit phrase meaning 'garland of islands', an apt description of their shape from above.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Near Kuala Lumpur a mature rainforest stands on former tin-mining ground. Researchers began planting the damaged land in the 1920s.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the Niah caves on Borneo, archaeologists found boat-shaped burials and a record of people using the rainforest stretching back at least 50,000 years.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Songket's shimmering patterns are woven into the cloth. Weavers introduce extra gold- or silver-coloured threads between the ordinary ones.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Oman’s aflaj move water by gravity. Communities have used observations of the sky to divide the available irrigation time among water users.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Dhofar, frankincense starts as resin from a tree. Trees, caravan stops and seaports preserve successive stages of its old trading route.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Oman's curved khanjar dagger is made by several crafts working together. Its distinctive outline also appears on the country's emblem.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: An inscribed pillar at Lumbini records a visit by Emperor Ashoka in the third century BCE to the site revered as the Buddha's birthplace.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Far below Nepal's snowy peaks, Chitwan's subtropical lowlands shelter one-horned rhinoceroses and Bengal tigers.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Eight of the world's ten highest peaks lie in or on the borders of Nepal. Everest and Kanchenjunga stand on different international frontiers.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: At Battir, stone terraces and irrigation channels share spring water among vegetable gardens. Families follow a customary rotation for their turn at the water.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Nablus, traditional soap starts with olive oil. Makers spread the cooked mixture across a floor, cut it into blocks and stack the blocks to dry.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Palestinian embroidery could once tell a viewer where its wearer came from. Colours and motifs on a dress carried local and family associations.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Moenjodaro, builders laid out a city of baked brick in the Indus Valley more than four thousand years ago. A street grid still shows through the ruins.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Kalasha observers use the shadows of the Hindu Kush as a calendar. The positions of the sun and stars against local peaks help set dates for sowing and festivals.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The boreendo is a small, hollow clay instrument of the Thar. A player can alter its tone simply by changing the angle at which they blow.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Sand covered the abandoned pearling port of Al Zubarah. Beneath it, archaeologists found traces of an entire Gulf town, from palaces to fishers' huts.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Among the rock carvings at Al Jassasiya are boats seen from above. Other carvings are rows of little cup-shaped hollows whose purpose is still debated.
options.label: qm.org.qa

options.text: Doha's name is usually traced to an Arabic word for a large tree. It may recall a landmark at the fishing village that preceded the capital.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The Arabian oryx disappeared from the wild and later returned to the sands of 'Uruq Bani Ma'arid through reintroduction.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Asir, women traditionally paint the inside walls of homes with bright geometric patterns. The house itself becomes the canvas.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Travellers crossing the desert at Ḥimā left their marks near its wells. Inscriptions in different scripts record people passing along the same route over centuries.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Singapore Botanic Gardens helped turn rubber into a Southeast Asian plantation crop. Research on this city plot had consequences across the region.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Singapore's hawker centres grew from street-food stalls into shared dining rooms. A game of chess or a busker can be as much a part of the scene as lunch.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Land reclamation has changed Singapore's island count in both directions. Some islands were joined together while entirely new ones were created.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Damascus glassblowers give broken glass another life. They melt the scraps in brick ovens and shape the molten glass on a hollow rod.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Bosra, a Roman theatre survives inside a later fortress. The seats look out from tiers of dark basalt.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In northern Syria, abandoned late-antique villages retain houses, churches and olive presses. They preserve the workings of whole farming communities.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A 660-tonne metal sphere hangs inside Taipei 101. Its motion helps steady the skyscraper when the wind makes the building sway.
options.label: www.taipei-101.com.tw

options.text: The Liwu River cut Taroko Gorge through marble as Taiwan's mountains rose. Rock that formed deep underground now makes the canyon walls.
options.label: www.taroko.gov.tw

options.text: On early European maps Taiwan often appears as Formosa. The name comes from Portuguese for 'beautiful'.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: At Dambulla, monks made shrines inside natural caves and covered the rock ceilings with paintings. The mountain itself forms the roof of the temple.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Anuradhapura grew around a sacred fig tree traditionally grown from a cutting of the tree under which the Buddha attained enlightenment.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Sri Lankan string puppetry is called rūkada nātya. Family troupes carve and dress their own wooden characters and bring them to life above a portable stage.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Between the Vakhsh and Panj rivers, floodwater sustains poplar forest in a dry Central Asian landscape. This riverside woodland is known as tugay.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The high ranges of Eurasia meet at the Pamir Knot in eastern Tajikistan. Several peaks in its national park top 7,000 metres.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Tajik oshi palav brings rice, vegetables and meat together in one pot. Learning to cook it can involve an apprenticeship with an experienced maker.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Water has a meaning beyond the famous splashing at Songkran. People also pour it over Buddha images and the hands of elders at Thai New Year.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In khon masked theatre, dancers become the monkey army and giant adversaries of the hero Rama. Singers and instrumentalists tell the story alongside them.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Phu Phrabat, prehistoric rock shelters became Buddhist sacred spaces. Upright boundary stones marked out places for religious ceremonies.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Timor-Leste names the same direction twice. Timor comes from a word meaning east, and leste is Portuguese for east.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Oecussi belongs to Timor-Leste but sits apart from the rest of the country on the Indonesian side of the island.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Timorese tais are handwoven textiles used for gifts, ceremonies and clothing. Their colours and motifs can identify the community that made them.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Sharjah, archaeological layers at Faya record repeated human occupation as the desert swung between dry and wetter periods over many thousands of years.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In oasis settlements, underground aflaj guide water to farms by gravity. Customary rules divide the flow among those who depend on it.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Fujairah's Hajar Mountains, Wadi Wurayah preserves rock from ancient oceanic crust and habitat for more than a thousand recorded species.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Merv was a succession of cities in one oasis. As rulers shifted the centre, the walls of earlier cities survived beside later ones.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A Turkmen dutar maker shapes a long-necked, two-stringed instrument. The same tradition encompasses building it, playing it and singing to it.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Akhal-Teke horse is bred in Turkmenistan and prized for its distinctive sheen. Breeders pass knowledge of pedigrees and training down through families.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Shibam, houses several storeys high rise from a walled town of mud brick. Building upwards kept the settlement compact on its floodplain.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Sana'a's tall rammed-earth and brick houses have pale geometric decoration that picks out windows and walls across the old city.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Ma'rib, the ancient kingdom of Saba channelled floodwater through a great dam to irrigate fields on both sides of a desert valley.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Archaeology at Tràng An records people adapting as the sea advanced and retreated among limestone towers. Some of today's inland cliffs once stood by the coast.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Quan họ singers trade verses between groups from different villages. One group offers a song and the other answers to a matching tune.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Hồ dynasty's citadel was built in the fourteenth century. Enormous fitted stone blocks still frame its gateways.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Uzbek askiya is a contest of wit. Speakers improvise on a shared topic, trying to outdo one another with wordplay.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Samarkand's location on the Silk Roads brought artisans and ideas together. The turquoise monuments of Timur's capital stand at that old crossroads.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Uzbekistan palov can turn cooking rice into work for an entire gathering. The dish is served at occasions ranging from weddings to commemorations.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Bohol, salt makers soak coconut husks in seawater for months, burn them and boil the resulting brine in pots. The finished salt looks like an egg in a shell.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Palawan a river runs through a limestone cave and empties directly into the sea. Tides reach into its lower underground stretch.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the Philippine Cordilleras, Ifugao farmers built irrigated rice terraces that follow the mountain contours. Forests above the paddies are part of the water system.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Bali's subak associations coordinate irrigation through networks of water temples. Decisions made upstream affect when farmers downstream can flood their rice terraces.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Balinese dance has sacred, semi-sacred and entertainment forms. The dance appropriate inside a temple can differ from the one performed for an audience outside.
options.label: ich.unesco.org

options.text: Lake Batur fills a volcanic crater and is regarded as a source of irrigation water. A major water temple stands beside the lake.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Macau's name is linked to A-Ma, a goddess who protects sailors. A bay and a temple at this old trading port bear her name.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Over Macau's port stands the Guia Lighthouse, identified by UNESCO as China's oldest lighthouse. It shares its hill with a fortress.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Macau's map once showed Taipa and Coloane as two separate islands. Reclaimed land between them joined them together.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Almonds helped date an ancient merchant ship wrecked off Kyrenia. Researchers used radiocarbon measurements of its cargo alongside those of the ship's timbers.
options.label: news.cornell.edu

options.text: Bellapais Abbey's Gothic cloisters stand on a mountainside above Kyrenia. A medieval Latin monastery overlooks a stretch of the eastern Mediterranean.
options.label: www.visitncy.com

options.text: Near the far tip of the Karpas peninsula, Greek and Turkish Cypriot institutions worked together to restore Apostolos Andreas Monastery overlooking the sea.
options.label: www.undp.org

options.text: The road linking South and North Ossetia goes through the Greater Caucasus. The Roki Tunnel carries it under the mountain divide.
options.label: www.ebrd.com

options.text: Ossetic belongs to the Iranian branch of Indo-European. Its closest linguistic relatives lie far beyond these Caucasus valleys.
options.label: www.iranicaonline.org

options.text: Follow the map north from Tskhinvali and settlements string out along the Great Liakhvi. The Little Liakhvi and Froni valleys branch through different parts of the region.
options.label: www.echr.coe.int

options.text: At Sangiran on Java, fossil finds have made it possible to trace human ancestors across a long stretch of the Pleistocene.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Borobudur's Buddhist monument climbs in terraces around a hill. Rows of perforated stupas surround the summit.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Yogyakarta, a ceremonial axis runs through the sultan's palace. The plan relates the city to Mount Merapi to the north and the Indian Ocean to the south.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Lake Toba fills the caldera of an immense eruption. The large island of Samosir inside the lake rose as the caldera floor rebounded.
options.label: volcano.si.edu

options.text: At Ombilin, colonial coal mining required more than shafts. A railway carried coal out of Sumatra's interior mountains to a port on the west coast.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Sumatran orangutans live in the island's tropical forests. These are among the few places on Earth where orangutans still occur in the wild.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A British sovereign base on Cyprus contains a wetland of international importance. Akrotiri's salt lake and marshes share the peninsula with the military base.
options.label: www.ramsar.org

options.text: Greater flamingos feed in the wetland at Akrotiri. The suitability of the lake for the birds changes as water levels fluctuate.
options.label: rsis.ramsar.org

options.text: Two British and two Cypriot commissioners were appointed to mark the boundaries of Akrotiri and Dhekelia after independence. The two areas sit apart from one another on the same island.
options.label: www.legislation.gov.uk

options.text: Jeju's haenyeo harvest seafood by diving on a single breath. The women surface with a distinctive whistling exhalation.
options.label: ich.unesco.org

options.text: The same lava that built Jeju also hollowed out routes underground. Lava tubes remain where molten rock drained away beneath a solid crust.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Jeju, people welcome the wind goddess Yeongdeung with rites for calm seas and a good catch, then mark her departure with a farewell ceremony.
options.label: ich.unesco.org

options.text: At Tiébélé, the walls of the royal compound are a canvas. Kassena women renew the painted decorations on the earthen houses.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Ironworkers at Douroula were extracting metal from ore by the eighth century BCE. Elsewhere in the country tall natural-draught furnaces still stand.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The stone walls of Loropéni are at least a thousand years old. This fortified settlement belonged to a network that controlled gold for trans-Saharan trade.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Among Cameroon's Bamoun, the Nguon includes a public trial of the king's governance. Ritual chiefs present criticisms collected from the community.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the Sawa Ngondo ceremony, a priest dives from a sacred canoe into the Wouri River. People gather on the banks to await the water oracle's message.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Dja River curves around nearly the whole Dja forest reserve. The water forms a natural boundary for a rainforest inhabited by gorillas and chimpanzees.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Burundi's royal drummers combine synchronised beats with leaps, songs and heroic poetry. A group arranges its drums around a central drum.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Rain falling in Burundi can head for opposite sides of Africa. The country straddles the watershed between the Nile and Congo systems.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The borders of the precolonial kingdom of Burundi in the nineteenth century already resembled those of the modern country.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The cape in Cabo Verde's name is not on the islands. It is a peninsula on the Senegalese mainland, hundreds of kilometres to the east.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In Cabo Verde's morna songs, departure, separation and the longing to return are recurring subjects in music shaped by island life.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Cidade Velha on Santiago was the first European colonial town built in the tropics. The layout of the old settlement still follows the river valley.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: São Tomé and Príncipe are mountaintops in the Gulf of Guinea. They belong to a chain of volcanoes rising out of the Atlantic.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: São Tomé's old agricultural estates are known as roças. Cocoa and coffee plantations became a defining feature of the island's inhabited landscape.
options.label: www.unesco.org

options.text: The two islands are named for very different figures. São Tomé honours Saint Thomas, while Príncipe's original name referred to a Portuguese prince.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Aka singers can improvise their individual parts while keeping four interwoven vocal lines going. The forest's hunting and camp life have songs of their own.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Forest elephants visit open clearings in the Sangha forest to feed on mineral-rich soil. These gathering places make an otherwise elusive animal visible.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The savannas of Manovo-Gounda St Floris lie where distinct African ecological zones meet. Its floodplains also offer waterbirds a refuge in the dry season.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the Sahara, the Ounianga lakes include both fresh and intensely salty water. Underground supplies keep them from vanishing in the desert heat.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Wind and water carved arches and canyons into the Ennedi sandstone. Some deep canyons hold water year-round in the middle of the Sahara.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Lake Chad used to be part of an enormous inland sea. The animals of the wetter Sahara included hippos, giraffes and elephants.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The equator misses every piece of dry land in Equatorial Guinea. Its mainland lies north of the line, while the island of Annobón lies south of it.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: On Bioko you can climb from lowland rainforest into a very different mountain forest on the same small island. Its slopes shelter distinctive island primates.
options.label: www.unesco.org

options.text: Equatorial Guinea's mainland and Bioko are separate enough that a voyage from one to the other passes the coast of another country, Cameroon.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Flamingos feed in the shallow alkaline lakes of Kenya's Rift Valley. Their movements link lakes that look completely separate on a map.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Thimlich Ohinga, communities built a stone enclosure without mortar to protect both people and livestock near Lake Victoria.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: For the Mijikenda, patches of coastal forest preserve the sites of old fortified settlements called kayas. Their ancestral significance helped keep the trees standing.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Grande Comore rises around Karthala, a broad active shield volcano. Its summit is cut by a complex of craters.
options.label: volcano.si.edu

options.text: Comorian perfume plantations grow ylang-ylang alongside other fragrant plants. The blossoms are distilled for their essential oil.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: The Comoros take their name from an Arabic word for the moon. The archipelago once connected trading routes between East Africa, India and the Middle East.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: On some earthen mosques in northern Côte d'Ivoire, the projecting buttresses are topped with pottery or ostrich eggs.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Attiéké looks rather like couscous, but its grains start as cassava. The makers ferment and granulate the root before steaming it.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Zaouli performances among the Guro, a carved mask and costume turn the dancer into a character. Percussion drives remarkably intricate footwork.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The striped-legged okapi lives in the forests of the Congo Basin. The Ituri reserve protects part of the range of this elusive giraffe relative.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Salonga protects a vast tract of rainforest reached chiefly by water. Among its inhabitants is the bonobo, an ape found only in this country.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Virunga encompasses volcanoes, mountain gorilla habitat and the snowy Rwenzori highlands within the same national park.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In a Djiboutian wedding tradition, the groom receives camel meat preserved in ghee. First he has to work out how to untie the elaborately wrapped container.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Lake Assal sits below sea level. Its shore is the lowest exposed land in Africa.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Ships sailing from the Indian Ocean to Suez pass Djibouti at the entrance to the Red Sea. A small stretch of coastline sits beside an intercontinental sea route.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The Bijagós islands form an active delta out in the Atlantic. Mudflats and mangroves link the islands as tides rise and fall.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Bijagós mudflats feed hundreds of thousands of migratory shorebirds. The surrounding waters also support manatees and sea turtles.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The capital's name does double duty. Bissau was added to the country's name to distinguish it from neighbouring Guinea.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In highland Asmara, Italian colonial planners gave modernist architecture room to experiment. The city retains cinemas, workshops and other buildings from that period.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Eritrea's name is a piece of its own map. It comes from the ancient Greek name for the Red Sea along its coast.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Asmara's modernist buildings stand more than two kilometres above sea level. Its highland setting is far removed from the Red Sea port below.
options.label: UNESCO
