options.text: Gedeo farmers stack crops vertically on the escarpment. Tall trees shade enset, a staple food plant, and coffee grows underneath.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Under the Oromo Gada system, responsibilities move between organised age groups. Leadership changes hands on an eight-year cycle.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Konso communities built stone terraces across steep dry hillsides. They retain soil and catch water for farming where rain runs off fast.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Oklo, uranium deposits sustained natural nuclear reactions about two billion years ago. Scientists recognised the reactors from an unexpected isotope ratio in the ore.
options.label: inis.iaea.org

options.text: Lopé contains savanna beside dense rainforest. This patchwork preserves evidence of past climate shifts as well as thousands of years of human activity.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Ivindo National Park, rapids and waterfalls break up rivers running through equatorial forest. Aquatic communities have evolved around these natural barriers.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The smallest country on the African mainland is shaped like a river corridor. Most of The Gambia follows its namesake river inland through Senegal.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Tiny Kunta Kinteh Island in the Gambia River changed hands repeatedly as European powers competed over Atlantic trade, including the trade in enslaved people.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the Manding Kankurang tradition, a masked figure clad in bark and leaves moves through the community during initiation rites.
options.label: ich.unesco.org

options.text: More than four-fifths of Lesotho stands above 1,800 metres. This mountain country fits entirely inside South Africa.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Water is one of Lesotho's major exports. Dams and tunnels in its highlands transfer water across the watershed to South Africa.
options.label: lhda.org.ls

options.text: Sehlabathebe in Lesotho and the Drakensberg park across the South African border protect different sides of the same high mountain landscape.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Liberia's name comes from the Latin for 'free'. Its nineteenth-century republic grew from settlements established for free and formerly enslaved Black people from America.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The pygmy hippopotamus lives in West African forest, including Liberia. It shares its name with the familiar river hippo but belongs to a different genus.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Liberia's capital commemorates an American president. Monrovia was named for James Monroe.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In Madagascar's dry country, rain has carved limestone into the needle-like ridges called tsingy. The maze shelters wildlife isolated between the rocks.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Zafimaniry craftspeople use wood for houses, furniture and intricately carved surfaces. Timber joints hold the traditional homes together.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Malagasy kabary speakers weave proverbs, riddles and wordplay into public speeches. Their performance can turn a family occasion into an exercise in poetry.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Lake Malawi's cichlid fishes have diversified into hundreds of species. Closely related fish occupy remarkably different niches along the same rocky shores.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Nsima begins as ground maize, stirred into thick porridge. Making it involves a whole chain of skills from tending the crop to sharing the meal.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Mount Mulanje rises abruptly out of southern Malawi's plains. The huge isolated mountain is also regarded as a dwelling place of spirits and ancestors.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Every seven years, communities at Kangaba replace the thatch on the House of Speech. The re-roofing brings oral histories into public performance.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Timbuktu was a university town as well as a desert trading centre. Scholars gathered around Sankore and the city's other mosques.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Tomb of Askia at Gao is a stepped pyramid made of earth. It commemorates a ruler of the Songhai Empire beside the Niger.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Banc d'Arguin the Sahara meets extensive tidal flats. Birds that breed as far away as northern Eurasia spend the winter feeding there.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Chinguetti and three other desert towns grew up to shelter caravans. Their compact streets also supported scholars and religious schools.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Mauritanian mahadra is a community school that can travel with its teachers and students, a form of education suited to nomadic life.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Le Morne's cliffs helped people escaping slavery hide on a peninsula in southwest Mauritius. The mountain became a symbol of their resistance.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Aapravasi Ghat in Port Louis, indentured labourers from overseas first set foot on the island. The surviving immigration depot marks that passage.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Rodrigues, sega tambour musicians use drums to lead songs in Creole. The singing, drumming and dancing are closely linked.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Producing argan oil involves cracking the hard nut, grinding the kernels and working the paste to release the oil. The tree grows in Morocco's southwest.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Marrakesh, storytellers, musicians and other performers make Jemaa el-Fna square into an open-air venue whose programme changes through the day.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Aït-Ben-Haddou, a group of earthen houses sits inside defensive walls. The fortified settlement stood along a caravan route between the Sahara and Marrakesh.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Chopi timbila ensembles play wooden xylophones of different sizes. Skilled makers tune individual keys before the instruments can play together.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Island of Mozambique once served as the capital of Portuguese East Africa. A small island offshore gave the entire modern country its name.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: In Makonde mapiko performances, carved masks transform dancers into recognisable characters. Movement and music tell an audience who has appeared.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Agadez, a tall minaret rises from a city built largely of earth. Projecting wooden beams give its sides a bristling outline.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Some communities in Niger maintain formal joking relationships. People entitled to tease one another use humour to ease tensions and reinforce ties.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Aïr Mountains rise like islands out of the Ténéré desert. Their extra moisture supports vegetation that cannot grow on the surrounding sand.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Kano's Durbar, thousands of horsemen parade with the emir to mark the Eid festivals. Riders and horses both wear elaborate regalia.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On the outskirts of Osogbo, a sacred forest protects shrines and sculptures dedicated to Osun, the Yoruba divinity associated with its river.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Ijele masquerade can tower several metres above its carrier. Musicians, attendants and other performers accompany the enormous moving figure.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Odzala-Kokoua's rainforest opens into swampy clearings known as bais. They draw animals out from under the canopy, including forest elephants.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Brazzaville and Kinshasa, capitals of two separate countries, face each other across the Congo River.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The centres of Congolese rumba face one another across a river. Musicians in Brazzaville and Kinshasa developed a shared urban dance tradition in two different countries.
options.label: ich.unesco.org

options.text: Nyungwe's mountain forest feeds two great river systems. Rain from different sides of the watershed can head for either the Congo or the Nile.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Rwandan Intore dancers move in formation in a performance recalling warriors. Poetry, singing and drumming accompany the choreography.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Nyamata a former church is preserved as a memorial to the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi. It is one of four sites inscribed together to commemorate the victims.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Ceebu jën, rice and fish cooked with vegetables, is closely associated with Saint-Louis. Its preparation and the way diners share the platter are both part of the tradition.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Ancient burial grounds in Senegal and The Gambia are marked with circles of upright laterite stones cut from nearby quarries.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Djoudj wetlands lie just south of the Sahara. For birds flying across the desert, the Senegal River delta offers a first major place to feed and rest.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The coco de mer palm in the Vallée de Mai produces the world's heaviest seed. Its huge double-lobed fruit once puzzled sailors who found it drifting at sea.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Aldabra's remote coral atoll supports an enormous wild population of giant tortoises. Much of the land surrounding its lagoon sits only a little above the tide.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Enslaved Africans in Seychelles once danced moutya at night away from plantation houses. Performers warm the goatskin drum near a fire before playing.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Bunce Island links Sierra Leone to the rice-growing coast of the United States. Enslaved people shipped from here carried agricultural knowledge across the Atlantic.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: In the Gola forest and on Tiwai Island, pygmy hippos share the Upper Guinean forest region with forest elephants and white-necked rockfowl.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Sierra Leone's name comes from Portuguese for 'Lion Mountains'. Sailors applied it to the mountains rising beside what is now Freetown.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: About two billion years ago a space rock struck near present-day Vredefort. Erosion has exposed the deep structure of the enormous impact site.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Barberton Makhonjwa Mountains preserve rock more than three billion years old. They offer a rare view of what Earth's early surface was like.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Before Great Zimbabwe rose to prominence, Mapungubwe traded with the Indian Ocean coast from deep in the southern African interior.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The pyramids at Meroë were built for rulers of Kush. This Nile kingdom had its own royal city and its own tradition of pyramid burial.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The isolated hill of Gebel Barkal was revered as the home of the god Amun. Temples stand at its foot beside the Nile.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Red and gold feature in the Sudanese wedding ritual al-jertiq. The bride may wear a red garment with a gold-embroidered silk toab, while the groom wears white.
options.label: ich.unesco.org

options.text: At Lion Cavern, people dug into the mountainside for red ochre tens of thousands of years ago. Pigment drew miners here long before modern iron extraction.
options.label: www.thekingdomofeswatini.com

options.text: Sibebe Rock outside Mbabane is an immense exposed granite dome. Its smooth face rises above the surrounding hills.
options.label: www.thekingdomofeswatini.com

options.text: Both Eswatini and the name of the Swazi people recall King Mswati II, who expanded and consolidated the kingdom in the nineteenth century.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: At Ngorongoro you can descend into a huge volcanic caldera and see grazing herds on its floor. Nearby Olduvai preserves evidence of early humans.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The great Serengeti migration follows changing access to water and grass. Wildebeest, zebras and gazelles move across the plains with predators following.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the Kondoa rock shelters, painted figures have survived under natural overhangs. Some of the sites still have ritual uses for nearby communities.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Koutammakou, Batammariba families build earthen tower houses called takienta. The houses give this part of northern Togo its distinctive skyline.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Among the Guin of southern Togo, taking a sacred stone marks the new year. The rite belongs to a cycle of ceremonies that lasts several months.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The country takes its name from a settlement on Lake Togo. The name likely combines Ewe words for water and shore.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In the Kerkennah Islands, fishers plant palm fronds in the seabed. The outgoing tide helps guide fish along these barriers into chambers and traps.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Roman amphitheatre at El Jem rises over a small Tunisian town. Its huge freestanding oval remains one of the clearest traces of Roman Africa.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Making harissa traditionally begins with drying red peppers in the sun. Families grind them with seasonings to make the paste.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Ugandan barkcloth makers beat the inner bark of the mutuba tree into fabric. A tree can regrow bark and yield another harvest.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Basoga bigwala music, individual gourd trumpets each sound a single note. A melody only appears when several players interlock their parts.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Rwenzori rise almost on the equator yet reach high enough for glaciers. Giant lobelias grow on their cold, wet mountain slopes.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: From space, a thin pale line crosses Western Sahara from Bou Craa towards the Atlantic. It follows a conveyor carrying phosphate rock from the interior.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Along Western Sahara's Atlantic shore, the desert fronts some particularly rich fishing grounds. The coast and the dry interior sustain very different livelihoods.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: A sand sea straddles the northern edge of Western Sahara. During dust storms, satellites can see airborne sand and dust travel offshore towards the Canary Islands.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Mine workers helped spread Zambia's Kalela dance. Dancers move in lines around drums and sing as they step forward and back.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the Makishi masquerade, costumed characters appear at the end of boys' initiation. Each mask represents a particular figure with its own role.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Victoria Falls the Zambezi spreads into a broad sheet before dropping into a narrow gorge. The rising spray gave it the name Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'the smoke that thunders'.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Great Zimbabwe's immense walls were built by fitting stones together without mortar. The modern country took its name from the ruined city.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Matobo, erosion has left heaps of rounded granite boulders balanced on one another. Rock shelters among them preserve paintings.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Mana Pools, channels left behind by the Zambezi fill and empty with its floods. They sustain wildlife along the valley floor in the dry season.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On La Gomera, Silbo Gomero carries spoken Spanish as whistles. A conversation can travel across ravines that would make a visit on foot a long journey.
options.label: ich.unesco.org

options.text: The laurel forest at Garajonay depends on moisture carried in by sea fog. It survives high on La Gomera above much drier slopes.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Tenerife's Mount Teide rises from the ocean floor. Measured from that submerged base, the volcanic edifice is much taller than its height above sea level.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Somali frankincense is harvested by tapping Boswellia trees. Different species yield distinct resins that traders recognise by name.
options.label: www.fao.org

options.text: Summer winds off Somalia can bring cold, nutrient-rich water to the sunlit surface. The monsoon helps feed ocean life as well as bringing rain to land.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: Medieval trading towns on the Somali coast linked the Horn to Arabia and Persia. The sea was a trade route between communities on opposite shores.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In Stone Town, builders used coral stone and lime for houses facing the Indian Ocean. Carved wooden doors became one of the port's signatures.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Zanzibar, taarab musicians perform at weddings whose festivities can run for days. Listeners know it as Swahili wedding music.
options.label: ich.unesco.org

options.text: Stone Town grew at the meeting point of African, Arabian, Indian and European trading networks. Those connections survive in the layout and buildings of a single port.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A sacred wooden xylophone in Guinea, the Sosso-Bala, is tied to the story of the Mali Empire. Its music accompanies the epic of Sunjata.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Mount Nimba, steep slopes and high grasslands rise above the surrounding forests. The mountain shelters an unusual live-bearing toad.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Niger begins in Guinea quite close to the Atlantic. From there it takes a long detour into the West African interior before reaching the ocean.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In Ghadamès, linked rooftops once gave women a route through the oasis town above the covered streets. The houses created two levels of circulation.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the rock art of Tadrart Acacus, animals and human activities change from one period to another. The images record a Sahara that was once much wetter.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Roman emperor Septimius Severus was born at Leptis Magna. He expanded his North African home city with monumental public buildings.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Laas Geel, artists painted cattle in elaborate neck decorations beneath rock overhangs. The shelters sit beside the route from Hargeisa to Berbera.
options.label: vr.africanrockart.britishmuseum.org

options.text: Laas Geel is part of a wider family of rock-art sites. Related depictions at Dhambalin and other shelters helped researchers recognise a regional painting style.
options.label: vr.africanrockart.britishmuseum.org

options.text: At trading sites around Berbera, archaeologists traced about nine-tenths of the imported ceramics they recorded to Asia. Pottery fragments reveal an Indian Ocean trade network.
options.label: www.incipit.csic.es

options.text: Vast herds of white-eared kob and other antelope migrate through the Boma and Badingilo landscape. From the air the moving herds stretch across the floodplain.
options.label: www.africanparks.org

options.text: The Sudd expands when the rains come. At high water this White Nile wetland can occupy an area equivalent to roughly fifteen per cent of South Sudan.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: South Sudan became independent in 2011. Its international border left the White Nile flowing north from one country into another on its way to Egypt.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Beginning in 2018, earthquake swarms off Mayotte led scientists to a newly formed volcano deep beneath the Indian Ocean.
options.label: www.brgm.fr

options.text: Mayotte's waters attract five species of sea turtle. Green and hawksbill turtles use the island's reefs, seagrass beds and nesting beaches.
options.label: ofb.gouv.fr

options.text: Mayotte's marine park protects an entire sequence of habitats. Mangroves line the shore, seagrass grows in the lagoon, and coral reefs stand farther out.
options.label: ofb.gouv.fr

options.text: Three immense natural amphitheatres, or cirques, cut deep into Réunion's volcanic interior. Steep enclosing walls separate valleys that look close on a map.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Enslaved Malagasy and African people helped create Réunion's maloya. The music combines singing, percussion and dance and has also served as a voice of protest.
options.label: ich.unesco.org

options.text: Piton de la Fournaise is an active shield volcano. Some eruptions have sent lava down Réunion's slopes all the way to the Indian Ocean.
options.label: volcano.si.edu

options.text: At Potosí, silver mining high in the Andes depended on artificial lakes. Aqueducts carried their water to the mills that crushed ore from Cerro Rico.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The centrepiece of Samaipata is an enormous outcrop transformed by carving. The ceremonial space was cut into the hill itself.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Kallawaya healers travelled through different Andean ecological zones to learn and practise their craft. Their knowledge of plants drew on environments far beyond a single valley.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Chinchorro fishing communities on the Atacama coast intentionally mummified their dead thousands of years before the celebrated Egyptian royal mummies.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Andean mining town of Sewell was so steep that stairs formed its main routes. Its copper miners lived in a town largely without streets for vehicles.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Chile's old nitrate works supplied fertiliser made from desert deposits. Humberstone and Santa Laura preserve whole industrial communities in one of Earth's driest regions.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Kaieteur Falls the Potaro River drops over a sandstone escarpment in one great plunge. The surrounding forest is home to a tiny golden frog.
options.label: guyanatourism.com

options.text: Guyana's links to South Asia run through its sugar plantations. After emancipation, indentured workers from India crossed the world to work there.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Guyana shares its historic regional name with Suriname and French Guiana. Its own territory was once known as British Guiana, while Suriname was Dutch Guiana.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Paraguayans prepare tereré with cold water and herbs crushed in a mortar. The mixture is poured over yerba mate and drunk through a filtering straw.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Piribebuy, a striped poncho is a team effort. Different weavers specialise in the body, fringes and finishing band.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Paraguay's guarania music takes its name from Guaraní culture. Its slow, syncopated melodies arose in the twentieth century and became a vehicle for songs of longing.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the forest beside the Suriname River, Jodensavanne preserves a seventeenth-century Jewish settlement with a synagogue, cemeteries and boat landings.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Paramaribo's historic centre translates European building plans into a local material. Much of this tropical capital's old architecture is made of wood.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Central Suriname Nature Reserve protects headwaters and mountains deep in the rainforest. Huge smooth granite domes rise abruptly above the canopy.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Near Atlántida, engineer Eladio Dieste made a church roof and walls undulate like waves. The material behind the curves is reinforced brick.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Fray Bentos became a familiar name on European tins because a factory on the Uruguay River turned cattle from the surrounding grasslands into meat extract and corned beef.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Montevideo's candombe, different-sized drums play interlocking parts. Marching drummers connect the tradition to particular streets and neighbourhoods.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Venezuela's tepuis are isolated flat-topped mountains. Angel Falls drops from one of their cliffs in Canaima National Park.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Corpus Christi, masked dancing devils participate in processions in several Venezuelan communities. The dance ends with their symbolic submission to the sacrament.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At the university campus in Caracas, architect Carlos Raúl Villanueva integrated modern art into the buildings. Alexander Calder's suspended forms hang over the main auditorium.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Rockets launched eastward from Kourou get a boost from Earth's rotation. French Guiana's proximity to the equator makes it a particularly effective place to launch satellites.
options.label: www.esa.int

options.text: The Îles du Salut once held a French penal colony. Today the islands have to be evacuated for rocket launches from the nearby spaceport.
options.label: centrespatialguyanais.cnes.fr

options.text: Far inland from the launch pads, French Guiana contains an Amazonian national park. Communities along the Maroni and Oyapock river systems are part of its lived landscape.
options.label: parc-amazonien-guyane.fr

options.text: The Falklands have rivers made of boulders. These stone runs are long bands of quartzite blocks left by Ice Age conditions, some stretching for kilometres.
options.label: falklands.gov.fk

options.text: Five kinds of penguin breed in the Falklands, including king, gentoo and southern rockhopper. They share the islands but use different nesting places.
options.label: falklands.gov.fk

options.text: Darwin met the Falklands' native wolf, the warrah, and predicted its disappearance. Within decades of his visit the animal was extinct.
options.label: falklands-museum.com

options.text: Around two thousand years ago, Hopewell builders in Ohio laid out immense earthworks in precise geometric shapes. Some of the alignments track the motions of the Moon.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Mesa Verde, Ancestral Pueblo builders fitted entire settlements into alcoves under sandstone cliffs. The rock face supplied both shelter and a back wall.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Poverty Point in Louisiana, hunter-gatherers built great earth mounds and concentric ridges. Monumental construction here did not depend on a farming economy.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Puerto Rico and San Juan effectively traded names. San Juan originally named the island, while Puerto Rico, or 'rich port', referred to its harbour settlement.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: On Vieques, tiny organisms light up when the water around them moves. At night, a paddle can leave a glowing trail through Mosquito Bay.
options.label: www.discoverpuertorico.com

options.text: The Arecibo telescope's giant dish sat in a natural sinkhole. Puerto Rico's limestone landscape provided the bowl for an instrument that listened to space.
options.label: www.nsf.gov

options.text: In San Pedro de Macorís, descendants of English-speaking Caribbean migrants developed Cocolo dance drama. The performances mix African-derived dance with plots from European traditions.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Dominican merengue is danced in couples. The accordion, drum and scraped güira give a typical ensemble its distinctive sound.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Santo Domingo's colonial city laid out a grid that Spanish planners subsequently used as a model elsewhere in the Americas.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Haitians serve joumou, a squash soup, on Independence Day. A dish associated with colonial exclusion became a meal shared to mark freedom.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The mountaintop Citadelle was built in the years following Haitian independence. Its commanding position was meant to defend the new country.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Haiti's compas grew into a dance music heard far beyond the country. Musicians of the Haitian diaspora helped carry it around the Caribbean and overseas.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Blue and John Crow Mountains sheltered people escaping slavery. Maroon communities developed routes and settlements in the rugged forested terrain.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In Moore Town's Maroon tradition, an abeng horn can send signals over a distance. The instrument recalls how communities communicated through the mountains.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Jamaican reggae grew from earlier local styles and borrowed sounds from abroad. Kingston's recording culture helped it travel around the world.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Trinidad's Pitch Lake is a natural reservoir of asphalt. Material reaching the surface can trap and preserve objects far older than the modern petroleum industry.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: Steelpan makers in Trinidad turned metal drums into tuned instruments. Different areas of a single steel surface sound different notes when struck.
options.label: www.unesco.org

options.text: Between 1845 and 1917, indentured workers from India crossed the Atlantic to Trinidad's sugar estates. Their descendants helped shape the country's culture.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: La Soufrière on Basse-Terre is an active volcano with a summit dome. Steam vents are a reminder that its plumbing is still hot.
options.label: volcano.si.edu

options.text: In Guadeloupean gwoka, singers, dancers and drummers face one another in a circle. The lead drummer responds to the dancer's movements.
options.label: ich.unesco.org

options.text: The Îlets Pigeon shelter reefs just off Guadeloupe's leeward coast. The national park extends underwater around these tiny islands.
options.label: www.guadeloupe-parcnational.fr

options.text: The pale turquoise around the Bahama Banks marks water shallow enough for sunlight to reach pale carbonate sand. Narrow deep channels stand out in dark blue.
options.label: science.nasa.gov

options.text: At Junkanoo, groups parade in costumes built and decorated by hand. Cowbells, drums and whistles carry the rhythm through the streets.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: On Andros, openings called blue holes lead into flooded limestone caves. Some lie inland, so you can encounter one well away from the coast.
options.label: www.bahamas.com

options.text: The Belize Barrier Reef system includes offshore atolls as well as the reef along the mainland. The water between them contains mangrove islands and seagrass beds.
options.label: whc.unesco.org

options.text: In Gales Point Manatee, Christmas Bram takes music and dancing from house to house. Sambai brings the community together around a central drum rhythm.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Belize was called British Honduras until 1973, but it is a separate country from Honduras. It faces the Caribbean across the Gulf of Honduras.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In the Diquís Delta, pre-Columbian craftspeople carved large stone spheres of remarkable precision. Some still mark the approaches to former settlements.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Costa Rica's painted oxcarts once hauled coffee to the Pacific. Distinct designs grew up in different regions, making some carts recognisable by their decoration.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Guanacaste protects a route from Pacific shore through tropical dry forest into cloud forest. Animals can move between sharply different climates within one conservation area.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Volcanic ash buried the farming community at Joya de Cerén. It preserved houses and domestic objects that show how ordinary families lived.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: El Salvador is the one Central American country whose entire seacoast faces the Pacific. It has no Caribbean shore.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In Panchimalco, the Confraternity of Flowers and Palms decorates palm fronds with flowers for a procession. Preparing them brings generations of neighbours together.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Sumpango and Santiago Sacatepéquez, communities build giant kites for the season of the dead. Elaborate pictures are assembled from coloured paper.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the Maya city of Tikal, tall temples rise through forest occupied by howler monkeys. The national park protects the ruins and their rainforest together.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Quiriguá, Maya sculptors carved immense stone stelae. Their inscriptions record dates and dynastic events in the city's own words.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: At Copán, Maya builders turned a staircase into a written monument. Carved glyphs run over the steps of its Hieroglyphic Stairway.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: The Río Plátano reserve follows a river from mountains to the Caribbean. Indigenous communities live within the protected forest landscape.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Honduras has two very unequal coasts. Its long Caribbean frontage contrasts with a short reach of Pacific shore on the Gulf of Fonseca.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: When León moved in the seventeenth century, the old town stayed behind. The ruins of León Viejo preserve the layout of an early Spanish colonial settlement.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In El Güegüense, a wily merchant outtalks colonial authorities. Masks, dance and satire keep the story alive in Nicaragua.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: León Cathedral's apparently simple outer walls hide a more elaborate interior. Its design reflects the need for a massive building to survive local earthquakes.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Coiba's isolation offshore helped it retain forest and animals lost from parts of the mainland. Reefs around the island belong to the same protected site.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Before there was a canal, mule trails and river routes carried goods across Panama. Their endpoints linked Caribbean shipping to the Pacific.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Makers of Panama's sombrero pintao process plant fibres into contrasting strips, then sew the braids into the distinctive patterned hat.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Steam and bubbling water fill Dominica's Boiling Lake. It occupies a flooded volcanic vent in Morne Trois Pitons National Park.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: In the Kalinago Territory, craftspeople preserve the tradition of making dugout canoes. A seagoing vessel begins as a single tree trunk.
options.label: legacy.discoverdominica.com

options.text: Dominica's European name records a day of the week. Columbus sighted the island on a Sunday in 1493.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Saint Vincent's botanical garden grows a breadfruit tree descended from one brought by Captain Bligh in 1793, on his successful voyage after the Bounty mutiny.
options.label: nationalparks.gov.vc

options.text: In 2021 La Soufrière went from slowly building a lava dome to explosive eruptions. Ash from Saint Vincent travelled to islands far downwind.
options.label: volcano.si.edu

options.text: The Grenadines do not all belong to the country that bears their name. Their southern islands form part of Grenada.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Gros Piton and Petit Piton are volcanic spires rising side by side near the sea. Their protected landscape extends down to reefs beneath the water.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Saint Lucia has rival flower societies, La Rose and La Marguerite. Each holds its own festival with a court of kings, queens and other officials.
options.label: ich.unesco.org

options.text: At Sulphur Springs, visitors can approach a volcanic geothermal field by road. Hot pools bubble and steam rises from the ground.
options.label: stlucia.org

options.text: At Carnival on Carriacou, rival performers recite Shakespeare in costume. Remembering lines from Julius Caesar belongs to a distinctly Grenadian tradition.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Wooden boatbuilders on Carriacou and Petite Martinique pass on their eye for a hull's shape through hands-on apprenticeship.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Grenada put one of its crops directly on its flag. The small emblem by the hoist is a nutmeg.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: At the Baths on Virgin Gorda, huge granite boulders lean together over the shore and make passages, pools and grottoes among the rocks.
options.label: www.bvitourism.com

options.text: Anegada is flat and made of coral limestone. It has a very different silhouette from the other main islands of the British Virgin Islands.
options.label: www.bvitourism.com

options.text: The RMS Rhone sank off Salt Island in a hurricane in 1867. Its wreck has become one of the territory's best-known dive sites.
options.label: www.bvitourism.com

options.text: On Salt Cay, workers used gates and wind-powered pumps to move seawater from pond to pond. Evaporation left crystals to rake for export.
options.label: www.visittci.com

options.text: The red top of the native Turk's cap cactus resembles a fez. The plant gave the Turks Islands their name and appears on their coat of arms.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: These islands once belonged administratively to Jamaica. Jamaica's independence in 1962 left Turks and Caicos a separate British colony.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: The blue iguana is native to just one island, Grand Cayman. The Salina Reserve protects habitat for this large, blue-grey reptile.
options.label: nationaltrust.org.ky

options.text: Cayman Brac takes its name from a Gaelic word for a bluff. A limestone escarpment running down the island makes it easy to see why.
options.label: trade.visitcaymanislands.com

options.text: The name Cayman preserves a word for crocodile. Europeans applied the Caribbean name for the animal to the islands.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Wooden sailing boats race as a national sport in Anguilla. Crowds can follow the contest alongshore as well as watching from the water.
options.label: ivisitanguilla.com

options.text: Anguilla's long, slender outline gave it its name. The word means eel in Spanish.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Anguillans resisted being governed together with Saint Kitts and Nevis. A revolt in the 1960s helped set the island on the road to separate administration.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Willemstad's Queen Emma Bridge floats on pontoons. It swings aside to let ships into the harbour, then returns so pedestrians can cross.
options.label: www.curacao.com

options.text: Willemstad grew in distinct districts around a deep natural harbour. Its buildings combine Dutch planning with Caribbean colours and materials.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Curaçao was once administered with other Dutch Caribbean islands as part of the Netherlands Antilles. In 2010 it became a constituent country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Enslaved Africans built Brimstone Hill Fortress on Saint Kitts. The volcanic hill and its great stone works commanded a wide stretch of Caribbean sea.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A channel called The Narrows separates Saint Kitts and Nevis. It is only about three kilometres across.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Kitts and Christopher are versions of the same name. The island's formal name, Saint Christopher, refers to the same place as Saint Kitts.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Until 1917 these islands were the Danish West Indies. The United States purchased Saint Thomas, Saint John and Saint Croix from Denmark.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: On Saint John, the Reef Bay trail leads to rock carvings beside a pool. They predate the island's colonial sugar works.
options.label: www.nps.gov

options.text: At Buck Island off Saint Croix there is a national park trail you follow by snorkel. Underwater signs guide swimmers through the coral reef.
options.label: www.nps.gov

options.text: At Maho Beach, arriving aircraft cross the shore just before touchdown. The runway of Princess Juliana International Airport begins almost at the sand.
options.label: www.vacationstmaarten.com

options.text: The border between Sint Maarten and French Saint Martin passes right across Simpson Bay Lagoon. Someone sailing across the lagoon can change jurisdictions without going out to sea.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Salt helped draw the Dutch to the island in the seventeenth century. The deposits were valuable enough for rival powers to contest them.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: In 1902 a fast-moving volcanic current from Mount Pelée destroyed Saint-Pierre. The disaster helped change how scientists understood explosive eruptions.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: Martinique's northern highlands preserve two volcanic landscapes of different ages, active Mount Pelée and the more deeply eroded Pitons du Carbet.
options.label: UNESCO

options.text: A Martinican yole has an unusual balancing system. The crew climbs out onto long poles to use their own body weight to keep the sailing boat upright.
options.label: ich.unesco.org

options.text: Saint Martin's name came from the calendar. Columbus sighted the island on 11 November, the feast day of Saint Martin of Tours.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: France and the Dutch Republic agreed to share the island in the seventeenth century. Its two present-day territories still meet along a land border.
options.label: CIA World Factbook (archived profile)

options.text: Off French Saint Martin, tiny islets such as Rocher Créole provide nesting places for seabirds. Their distance from the busy main island makes a difference to the birds.
options.label: reservenaturelle-saint-martin.com

options.text: The Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes got its name after the 1912 Novarupta eruption. Water heated beneath the fresh deposits escaped through thousands of steaming vents.
options.label: www.nps.gov

options.text: During the Ice Age, lower seas exposed land between Alaska and Siberia. Much of that former land bridge now lies underneath the Bering and Chukchi seas.
options.label: home.nps.gov

options.text: At Brooks Falls, brown bears wait on the lip of the waterfall while salmon try to jump upstream. The obstacle brings bears and fish to exactly the same spot.
options.label: www.nps.gov
